title: Clean Great Loop URLs return cache-dependent 404s and self-redirects
confidence: high for responses; medium for cache involvement; origin cause unverified
evidence: Of 720 sitemap URLs, 121 returned 404 and 22 ended in self-301 loops. Across the expanded crawl, 195 failed Great Loop URLs were rechecked with ?fpw_seo_audit=20261025: 178 returned 200 and 17 remained 404. For example, the 92nd Street bridge returned 301 Location equal to its own requested HTTPS URL, CF-Cache-Status HIT (Age 14773 on repeated hops); its query variant returned 200. Aberdeen returned a cached 404 while its query variant returned 200. See cache-rechecks.csv for every pair. Query behavior and cache headers establish response inconsistency, not the exact Cloudflare/origin misconfiguration.
impact: Ordinary visitors and crawlers following clean links can fail to reach otherwise available planning references. The observations do not prove when this began or explain the export-period traffic change.
safest_fix: After reviewing effective production rules, use a narrowly scoped cache bypass for affected public library paths if it is confirmed to restore correct responses; repair the specific bad rule and invalidate only affected cache entries under separate implementation authorization.
best_fix: Reconcile Cloudflare cache keys, redirects, proxy HTTPS handling and deployed IIS rewrite rules. Establish one clean-URL response contract, correct its root cause, then remove contaminated cached responses and verify that fresh responses stay correct. Do not remove the 178 recoverable pages from the sitemap as if they were retired.
estimated_effort: 1–3 days investigation and repair; depends on configuration access
dependencies: Read-only effective CDN/IIS configuration, deploy history and origin logs; implementation approval
risks: A broad purge or blanket bypass can mask the cause, increase load or disturb private cache rules. Do not change application data to compensate for cached errors.
post_fix_verification: Retest all 195 clean/query pairs with bounded GETs after authorized changes; valid pages should give stable 200 and clean canonicals, with no self Location or HTTPS downgrade. Repeat after cache warming; inspect verified crawler logs if available.

title: Seventeen sitemap port URLs remain 404 on both requests
confidence: high for 404 and sitemap inclusion; retirement intent unverified
evidence: All 17 persistent failures are listed in persistent-port-404s.csv. Clean and diagnostic-query requests both return 404; the page says the port is unavailable. The source resolves ID, then slug, then the existing port_slug_redirects mapping before returning 404. Production records/mappings were not inspected, so missing, retired and mismapped records cannot be distinguished.
impact: The sitemap promotes unavailable destinations and may send users to a dead end. Some similarly named surviving ports exist, but a name alone is insufficient evidence for a replacement.
safest_fix: Confirm retirement intent for these exact 17 URLs; remove intentionally unavailable URLs from the sitemap and relevant links while retaining a true 404/410.
best_fix: Reconcile each old record with its correct current entity. Use the existing redirect mechanism for a verified equivalent only, retain 404/410 where none exists, and synchronize sitemap and links. Keep the investigation separate from the recoverable cache failures in SEO-001.
estimated_effort: 0.5–1.5 days after record ownership is clear
dependencies: Production port and redirect mapping read access; content owner
risks: Wrong redirects can send boaters to a different city or waterway. Do not redirect all missing ports to home or the library hub.
post_fix_verification: Every removed URL is absent from sitemap; each approved replacement uses one permanent redirect to a 200 canonical page; truly retired pages retain a correct error status.

title: Production redirect behavior diverges from repository rules
confidence: high for live behavior and source difference; deployed cause unverified
evidence: Direct /index.cfm and /INDEX.cfm return 200 with a root canonical. http://www.floatplanwizard.com/ redirects to https://floatplanwizard.com/index.cfm, which remains 200. Slashless HTTPS calculator and trip-planning URLs redirect first to HTTP and then back to HTTPS. Direct directory index variants also return 200 with clean canonicals. Repository web.config contains root-index, host, HTTPS and clean-route rules, but the effective deployed configuration is unavailable.
impact: Unnecessary hops and alternate entry URLs complicate consolidation and delay access. Correct canonical tags mitigate several duplicates; there is no proof Google selected the wrong canonical.
safest_fix: Correct only the demonstrated HTTPS downgrade and root-index cases in the effective production rule layer, preserving request guards and semantic query parameters.
best_fix: Review rule precedence across CDN and IIS and normalize host, scheme and applicable aliases directly to the intended HTTPS canonical in one redirect. Maintain a separate equivalent test matrix for Tomcat development routing.
dependencies: Effective IIS and CDN rules; avoid copying IIS rules into Tomcat
risks: Redirecting internal rewrites without THE_REQUEST-style guards can create loops. Preserve legitimate parameters and /fpw development mount.
post_fix_verification: Test HTTP/HTTPS, www/non-www, slash/no slash, explicit indexes, legacy .cfm, case and query variants. Require no HTTPS-to-HTTP hops and no loop; preserve meaningful query strings.

title: Public legacy app routes compete with clean canonical pages
confidence: high for conflicting signals; ranking effect unverified
evidence: The legacy public fuel page returns 200 without a canonical or description; robots.txt allows it. The app lock library and Olmsted detail return 200 with self-canonicals, while the clean versions separately self-canonicalize. Source branches on isCleanLockRoute to create these competing canonical targets.
impact: Duplicate public route families provide inconsistent consolidation signals. Keyword cannibalization and lost rankings are hypotheses, not demonstrated effects.
safest_fix: If the content is equivalent, canonicalize legacy app routes to the verified clean public counterparts while preserving member actions and existing links.
best_fix: Audit whether any legacy route has distinct functionality or parameters; permanently redirect truly redundant public GET routes to clean equivalents, otherwise retain the route with a consistent canonical and aligned structured-data URLs.
dependencies: Confirm route equivalence and member entry behavior; SEO-001 reliability
risks: A blanket /app redirect could break authenticated workflows, API callers or useful filters.
post_fix_verification: Legacy/public pairs resolve or canonicalize to the same 200 target; source, rendered HTML and JSON-LD agree; member navigation and meaningful parameters still work.

title: Shared navigation still sends visitors through legacy aliases
evidence: Live navigation and footer link to /boat-fuel-calculator/boat-fuel-calculator.cfm; footer Help links to /app/help.cfm. Those routes redirect to public destinations. Local active top_nav.cfm already uses the clean fuel path, while the local footer retains the legacy aliases. This is a confirmed source/live discrepancy for the navigation link, not proof that all local files are deployed.
impact: Sitewide links pay redirect costs and reinforce aliases. A source-only edit could duplicate a change already present locally and fail to address deployment.
safest_fix: Verify which active navigation version is deployed; publish the already-correct link where appropriate and narrowly update the footer targets using the existing base-path variable.
best_fix: Align active shared navigation/footer with the verified canonical route map and add a focused deployed-link check to the existing release verification process.
dependencies: Resolve source/live version mismatch; SEO-003 final route map
risks: Preserve auth hooks, labels, analytics attributes and /fpw versus root behavior; do not refactor navigation.
post_fix_verification: Inspect real rendered hrefs on home, guide and calculator at mobile/desktop; clean links reach final 200 destinations directly in each environment.

title: Exclusion directives are uneven across Follow shells and a public mockup
confidence: high for observed directives; intended mockup availability requires owner confirmation
evidence: Anonymous Follow shells return 200 without HTML robots or X-Robots-Tag noindex; their paths are disallowed in robots.txt. The source applies noindex to Follow preview mode only. /family.cfm is a 200 Voyage Stream Mockup with no exclusion directive and no matching robots disallow. No private token or trip was accessed. The member manual correctly returns noindex,nofollow; completed-trip/preview exclusions are source-only checks.
impact: Crawl blocking alone does not ensure a URL will never appear in search. The mockup could be discovered as an unintended public result. No actual private indexing or disclosure was demonstrated.
safest_fix: Add noindex at the existing response/template boundary for intentionally non-searchable public shells; apply it to the mockup if it must remain accessible. Keep authentication and token validation intact.
best_fix: Document intended indexing per route family, enforce noindex consistently for non-searchable responses, and withdraw the prototype if it has no approved public purpose. Decide crawler access narrowly after reviewing any actual indexed URLs; do not broadly remove private robots restrictions.
dependencies: Owner decision on mockup; source review of all response modes; implementation approval
risks: A noindex directive cannot be read by a crawler blocked from fetching the URL. Robots is not access control. Do not index private trip pages or loosen authentication.
post_fix_verification: Verify unauthenticated, invalid-token and explicitly authorized preview responses without exposing private data; inspect headers/meta and access controls. Use Search Console existing records to establish whether unwanted URLs are indexed.

title: Sitemap coverage, PDF canonicals and modification dates need one policy
confidence: high for listed mismatches; indexing effect unverified
evidence: The static sitemap contains 720 URLs, including seven solo pamphlet PDFs whose HTTP Link canonical points to the HTML solo guide. It lists only the anchorage hub, while 218 additional direct clean anchorage pages returned 200 in the crawl (further failed URLs recovered in query rechecks). Emergency-guide sitemap lastmod is 2026-08-22 while Article dateModified is 2026-08-23; the visible reviewed date is August 22. No sitemap generator was identified. Dates do not by themselves establish which revision date is correct.
impact: Canonical signals and sitemap membership are inconsistent; useful reference coverage and lastmod maintenance are uneven. Sitemap omission does not prove a page is undiscovered or unindexed.
safest_fix: Review canonical intent: if the HTML guide is preferred, remove the seven noncanonical PDF entries while keeping downloadable links. Add only vetted, canonical, stable-200 anchorage pages and correct dates from actual content-change evidence.
best_fix: Use a documented canonical public-URL manifest or existing publishing workflow to produce a validated sitemap from published records, with truthful significant modification dates and exclusion rules. A generator is a later scoped implementation, not part of this audit.
estimated_effort: 0.5–1 day manual alignment; 1–3 days for a separately approved generator
dependencies: SEO-001/002 stable URLs; content owner; PDF indexing policy
risks: Do not add filter permutations, diagnostic queries, unreviewed port rows or private pages. Never set all lastmod dates to today or noindex all PDFs automatically.
post_fix_verification: Sitemap URLs are final canonical 200 targets, dates match meaningful changes, intended PDFs retain extractable text and correct headers; compare eligible public records with sitemap output.

title: Large raster assets create avoidable mobile transfer weight
confidence: high for bytes; field performance effect unverified
evidence: In the 390px controlled browser samples, the fuel CSS image transferred 1,575,850 bytes, signup CSS image 1,613,513 bytes, and home preview plus background 778,629 + 486,249 bytes. The same asset URLs are used at desktop size. The 14 initial render samples had no page overflow and initial CLS 0; no field CWV or Lighthouse score was obtained. Two-page pamphlet PDFs are also about 1.26 MB, despite being text-extractable.
impact: Large downloads can burden mobile visitors before tool use or registration, especially on slower links. This is a byte-weight opportunity, not proof of poor field LCP or conversion loss.
safest_fix: Compress/resize the specific heavy assets with visual review, preserve layout dimensions and existing CSS hooks, and avoid lazy-loading the actual LCP element.
best_fix: Provide appropriately sized modern-format variants with responsive selection and a fallback, prioritizing fuel and signup. Optimize PDF image payloads separately without damaging text, print quality or accessibility.
dependencies: Original assets and approved appearance; baseline image snapshots
risks: Overcompression can damage UI screenshots and printed emergency cards. Broad CSS/image refactors are unnecessary.
post_fix_verification: Compare transferred bytes and screenshots at 390px/1440px; repeat controlled loading under a stated network profile and review field CWV when supplied. Verify no layout shifts, lost text or form changes.

title: Fuel-page click loss is measurable; its cause is unresolved
confidence: high for arithmetic; low for causal attribution
observed_at: Exports inspected 2026-10-25; exported absolute periods unknown
evidence: Fuel clicks fell 56 to 29 (-48.2%), impressions 12,028 to 9,962 (-17.2%), and computed CTR 0.466% to 0.291%; exported position improved 5.90 to 5.67. This accounts for 27 of the 43 fewer page-row clicks (62.8%). The query export has 0 current clicks and only 678 impressions, versus device totals 110 and 16,837. Absolute dates, property identity and daily data are absent.
impact: The largest organic landing-page opportunity is losing clicks, but position alone cannot identify query mix, seasonality, SERP changes or technical causation. Rewriting an already relevant title without query evidence may miss the cause.
safest_fix: Obtain dated daily/page/query/device exports and isolate the fuel page before changing copy. Keep the existing useful free-tool title and task explanation while investigating.
best_fix: Diagnose equal finalized date windows plus year-over-year cohorts and deployment/error chronology. Once supported, test one specific snippet or tool-entry improvement and evaluate qualified engagement/registration with defined analytics events.
estimated_effort: 0.5–1 day analysis once data is available; experiment duration depends on traffic
dependencies: Exact export requests in report; no GA4 conversion definitions supplied
risks: Very low click counts and missing queries can produce unstable conclusions. No promised recovery, seasonality claim or hosting attribution.
post_fix_verification: Recalculate CTR from totals; compare like-for-like dates, query/device/country mix and field landing behavior. Record a hypothesis and measurement window before any copy test.

title: Public port references expose unreviewed seed records
confidence: high for published placeholders; record corrections require review
evidence: Kingston, Jamaica is publicly presented as a Great Loop port with loop segment and waterway Needs Review and coordinates in Jamaica. Columbus, Ohio has the same review placeholders. Of 142 successful direct port-detail URL responses in the base crawl (includes one alias), 141 say approach notes have not been verified; eight contain Needs Review. Even the Kingston, NY page says services and approach notes are unverified. These counts describe fetched responses, not all database entities. The source lookup by ID/slug does not require a reviewed publication status.
impact: A search visitor looking for a useful Great Loop stop receives seed provenance and placeholders, sometimes for an evidently mismatched place. Accurate city disambiguation and useful local detail matter more than expanding the number of indexable records.
safest_fix: Have the content owner classify suspect/unreviewed records and temporarily exclude confirmed unsuitable pages from search/public lists using an approved publication rule; retain any needed internal planning records. Do not mass-delete or merge by name.
best_fix: Introduce a narrowly scoped reviewed-publication gate for port references and sitemap eligibility. Verify location/entity, route relevance and source-backed services/approach notes, then publish concise useful content with state/country disambiguation in title/H1. Use real equivalents for approved consolidations.
estimated_effort: 1–2 days for gating/design; editorial review varies by record
dependencies: Authoritative location/port sources, production record access, owner decisions; SEO-002 reconciliation
risks: Existing waypoints may reference IDs. Data deletion or automatic geography correction is outside scope. A generic disclaimer does not verify a record.
post_fix_verification: Spot-check reviewed records against sources; excluded records are absent from public sitemap/listing and have the intended response directives; internal waypoint use is preserved; names and canonical identities are unambiguous.

title: Lock template labels secondary references as official sources
confidence: high for label mismatch; operational data accuracy not determined
evidence: The shared detail template always titles the section Official Source and the link Open official source. Pickwick points to waterwayguide.com/lock/5-33/pickwick-locks-and-dam, a secondary reference; Olmsted points to USACE. The template does not distinguish authority links from secondary guides. This audit did not validate every phone, VHF channel or operating schedule.
impact: The label overstates the authority of some references, reducing clarity where boaters need to verify current operational information.
safest_fix: Use a neutral Source / reference label for the existing source_url field and retain the visible instruction to verify with the official authority.
best_fix: Distinguish actual authority/contact links from secondary reference links in reviewed records and render accurate labels. Add current authority sources where missing, without claiming live status.
estimated_effort: 1–3 hours for neutral wording; record review separately scoped
dependencies: Content/source ownership; no new schema or data model required for narrow fix
risks: Do not replace valid secondary sources with guessed official URLs or alter operational facts without verification.
post_fix_verification: Inspect Pickwick and an actual USACE-backed page; labels match provenance, existing URLs and safety caveats remain intact; source review dates represent real review.

title: Reference pages can better connect research to the existing planning workflow
confidence: high for available content; conversion effect unmeasured
evidence: The trip-planning guide already has screenshots, a Chicago/Starved Rock research example, geometry-based per-leg NM overrides, explicit lock-time limitations and a manual fuel-calculator handoff. Lock detail related links emphasize fuel/safety; the guide is available in global navigation but has no equivalent contextual link in that planning paragraph. Source confirms geometry-derived override distance and separate idle hours/fuel handling; authenticated runtime was unavailable.
impact: A specific next-step link may help reference visitors learn how to use the tool before registering. There is no measured funnel or registration-lift evidence.
safest_fix: Add one contextual link from a relevant lock planning paragraph to the existing guide section, preserving all action hooks and current CTAs.
best_fix: Use a small number of accurate contextual handoffs: lock reference to timing guidance, path review to saved geometry/NM, corrected daily distance to manual fuel check, then reviewed route to Float Plan. Reuse the existing guide rather than create overlapping thin articles.
dependencies: Confirm deployed guide/source alignment; no new product promises
risks: Do not describe a numeric mileage input, automatic lock-delay timeline adjustment, live lock queues or automatic public-calculator synchronization; current guide explicitly says otherwise.
post_fix_verification: Check anchors, meaningful link text, desktop/mobile placement and base paths; verify wording against current controls before implementation; measure only with agreed existing analytics definitions.
